front_matter: Copper−Iron-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling of ortho-Substituted Sulfonamides with Sterically Hindered (Hetero)aryl Chlorides and Alkyl Halides: Synthesis of Sulfonamide Drugs

Keya Roy, Anay Saha, Sampa Mondal, and Laksmikanta Adak* In recent decades, palladium-catalyzed coupling reactions have been widely employed to facilitate the coupling reaction of primary sulphonamides with aryl halides, typically in the presence of bulky phosphine ligands (Scheme 1a).8a−g These

aReaction conditions: (heteo)aryl or alkyl sulfonamides (0.5 mmol), (heteo)aryl or alkyl halides (0.75 mmol), Fe(acac)3 (5 mol %), CuI (5 mol %), K2CO3 (0.75 mmol), DMSO (100 μL for 0.5 mmol scale of reaction) under N2 atmosphere. Isolated yields are reported.

successfully provided the desired products (2−9) in high yields.15 The reaction of 2-chloroanisole with benzenesulfonamide using a copper catalyst in the presence of a ligand was previously attempted, but resulted in a trace amount of the product 3.10a This observation showcases the efficiency of our established catalytic system toward deactivated aryl chlorides. We extended our protocol to more challenging conditions by introducing steric bulk to both coupling partners. We were pleased to find that our developed methodology performed with high success in reactions between coupling partners possessing sterically hindered ortho substituents, yielding the products 10− 20 in high yield, highlighting the exceptional compatibility of our method with steric challenges. Notably, several aryl chlorides and bromides bearing substituents at the ortho, meta, and para positions successfully underwent coupling

aReaction conditions: aryl or alkyl sulfonamide (0.5 mmol), (hetero)aryl chloride or bromide (0.75 mmol), Fe(acac)3 (5 mol %), CuI (5 mol %), K2CO3 (0.75 mmol), DMSO (100 μL for 0.5 mmol scale of reaction), under N2 atmosphere. Isolated yields are reported.

reactions with meta- and para-substituted arylsulfonamides as well as polyaromatic sulfonamides, yielding products 21−27 in good to excellent yields. It is notable that 1,2-dibromobenzene and 1,3,5-tribromobenzene underwent selective cross-coupling with aryl sulfonamides, affording products 7, 14, and 21 in excellent yields. The retained bromide groups in these products indicate their suitability for subsequent cross-coupling processes, thereby broadening the possibilities for further chemical modifications.

The coupling reaction was investigated with diverse heteroaromatic structures for both coupling partners (Scheme 2). (Hetero)aryl chlorides and bromides reacted successfully with (hetero)arylsulfonamides, providing N-heteroaryl sulfonamides 28−34 with 61−83% yield. The protocol was not restricted to single heteroaromatic coupling partners, as the optimal reaction condition was efficiently applied for the coupling reaction of heteroaromatic primary sulfonamides with heteroaryl chlorides and bromides, providing highly enriched heteroatomic structured secondary sulfonamides 35− 37 with moderate to good yield. The coupling reactions are not limited to aromatic or heteroaromatic substrates; they also proceeded effectively with sterically hindered aliphatic primary sulfonamides and challenging alkyl chlorides and bromides, as well as styryl bromide, to produce coupling products 38−46 in high yields (Scheme 2). These results highlight the wide applicability and robust nature of this methodology.

Finally, to demonstrate the practicability of this novel copper−iron-catalyzed method and its potential application for the synthesis of commercially available drugs and drug-like molecules, we prepared a range of pharmaceutically established secondary sulfonamide drugs5a−c,9b,h,10a,16 (Scheme 3).

In this study, it was observed that 4-amino benzenesulfonamide underwent a highly selective C−N cross-coupling reaction, leaving the primary amine group intact. This selectivity toward C−N coupling in the presence of multiple nucleophilic NH2 groups enabled the efficient synthesis of antibiotic, antimicrobial, and antimalarial drug molecules 47−56 with good yields. Aryl chlorides and bromides, bearing trifluoromethyl and other sensitive functional groups including nitro, acyl, ester, and vinyl, are well tolerated, resulting in biologically and medicinally demanding secondary sulfonamides (57−65) with yields of up to 89%. Furthermore, our optimal cross-coupling strategy was effectively employed in the synthesis of Dabrafenib (66), an anticancer drug, achieving an 81% yield, and Dofetilide (67), an antiarrhythmic drug, which was obtained in 89% yield. These results highlight the practical utility of our methodology in pharmaceutical synthesis.

To showcase the practical utility of the cross-coupling reaction, a synthesis on a gram scale was conducted under the optimized reaction conditions, affording the desired secondary sulfonamide product 13 in a comparable yield within the same time period relative to the lower millimolar reaction scale.14b

To assess the practical applicability of the protocol, we carried out several synthetic transformations using our synthesized cross-coupled products 1,14c 14, 31, and 54. The products 14 and 54 (antimicrobial drug) underwent further cross-coupling with benzenesulfonamides under the optimized reaction conditions, affording the extended cross-coupled products 68 and 69 in 62% and 58% yield, respectively (eqs 1 and 2). Moreover, we employed product 31 in C−H functionalization reactions where the quinoline moiety acts as a directing group. Under cobalt catalysis, compound 31 underwent efficient C(sp2)−H iodination, while palladium catalysis facilitated C(sp2)−H selenylation, yielding products 70 and 71, respectively, in 71% and 42% yields (eq 3). The catalyst was successfully reused for up to five consecutive cycles without significant loss of catalytic activity.14d To investigate the mechanism of the cross-coupling reaction, preliminary mechanistic studies were conducted. As an initial approach, a radical clock experiment was performed under standard reaction conditions employing 1-(allyloxy)-2-chlorobenzene as a radical probe (eq 4). This experiment yielded the direct cross-coupling product 72 without generating a ringclosed cross-coupling product, indicating that radical intermediates are not generated in the reaction. Subsequently, the reaction was conducted in the presence of a few radical scavengers, and a noteworthy amount of product 1, was still isolated, further supporting the conclusion that the reaction proceeds through a nonradical pathway.14e A series of experiments were carried out to identify the oxidation state of the active catalytic species participating in the mechanistic cycle and to explore the reaction mechanism. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was utilized to perform the high-resolution Fe 2p spectrum of the sample.14f This experiment confirms the presence of Fe(II) and Fe(III) oxidation states in the reaction mixture.13a,17 Furthermore, the experiment also suggests that Cu is present in the +1 oxidation state within the active catalytic species.14g,13a,18 UV spectroscopy was analyzed which supports the presence of Fe(II), Fe(III), and Cu(I) species in the reaction mixture.14h Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis of the residual powder, collected after extracting the organic compounds,14i indicated the existence of both Fe(II) and Fe(III) species, along with Cu(I).13a,19 Based on mechanistic studies and prior literature reports,10d−f,20 a plausible mechanistic pathway is proposed in Scheme S2. The proposed reaction mechanism proceeds through three elementary steps: (i) The aryl halide undergoes oxidative addition to the catalytically active copper(I) species A, generating intermediate B.10d−f,20 The sulfonamide substrate or acetylacetonate (acac) might coordinate with the active catalytic species, potentially assisting in the oxidative addition process. (ii) transmetalation of intermediate B with an iron-amide species to yield intermediate C;21 and (iii) reductive elimination from intermediate C to produce the cross-coupling product and to regenerate the involved active copper(I) species A.

In summary, we report the first efficient copper−ironcatalyzed cross-coupling reaction of sterically hindered (hetero)aryl chlorides and bromides with ortho-substituted primary sulfonamides under solvent-minimized conditions and in the absence of any externally added ligand. This method was successfully extended to a broad range of aryl, heteroaryl, and alkyl chlorides and bromides, as well as various primary heteroaryl-, aryl-, and aliphatic sulfonamides. It demonstrates a wide scope of substrates with 104 examples and shows excellent compatibility with various sensitive functional groups, including −COCH3, −CO2Me, −CO2Et, −CN, −NO2, −NH2, −Br, −Cl, −F, −CF3, −OCF3, −OCH3, −CH2Ph, vinyl, and heterocycles. Notably, this approach allows for selective C−N cross-coupling reaction despite the presence of multiple nucleophilic NH2 groups, preserving the primary amine functionality. Additionally, the method has been effectively utilized in the synthesis of 10 commercially available sulfonamide-based drugs and 11 pharmaceutically important scaffolds, highlighting its significance in medicinal chemistry. Several synthetic transformations, such as further cross-coupling and C−H functionalization, were performed using our synthesized cross-coupled products. The protocol is also applied to gram-scale synthesis, demonstrating its practicality for larger-scale applications. Moreover, this protocol avoids the need for conventional workup procedures, enhancing overall efficiency and simplicity. Importantly, the catalyst employed is environmentally benign, cost-effective, and demonstrates reusability for at least four reaction cycles. The reaction mechanism for the cross-coupling was also investigated.
